units.la: ILLUSTRI ET MAGNIFI-CO DOMINO, JOHANNI SKUMIN LITHUANO, CAPITANEO BRAS-EAVVIENSI, Fortunatus Crellius, Philosophus
units.tr: To the illustrious and magnificent lord, John Skumin, Lithuanian, captain of Braslav: Fortunatus Crellius, Philosopher

units.la: CUi dono Veterem nouum Libellum, nouam de re Veteri-noua disputationem? tibi, Jo-hannes illustis. nam tu & nos, & nostra soles adamare.
units.tr: To whom should I dedicate this old-and-new little book, this new disputation on an old-and-new subject? To you, illustrious John, for you are accustomed to love both us and what is ours.

units.la: Ex quo enim ad nos appulisti, statim, nulla interposita mora, Logicos nostros, quos è limpidissimo fonte deduximus, riuulos, cum generoso Slopecio, & alijs, tibi degustādos existimasti. quos ita degustasti: ut penitus eos exhausis-se videare, probat id perennis nostra disputandi ratio,
units.tr: For from the time you came to us, without any delay at all, you judged that our logical rivulets, which we drew from the clearest spring, were worth tasting by you, together with the noble Slopecius and others. And you tasted them so thoroughly that you seem to have drained them dry. Our ever-flowing manner of disputing proves it.

units.la: Instructus acie Logica jam in ipsa Na-turae arcana vis intueri. prudentissime. nosti enim, quid generosos & Magnificos, quid illustres & principes Viros deceat, quid ad feliciter imperandum re-quiratur. nosti, quid olim sapientissimi homines, quid Plato, quid Aristoteles, de rerumpub. & regnorum felicitate pronunciarint, felices illas respub. esse, quarum gubernacula vel Philosophi tenent, vel qui philosophantur. cui rei vel præsens, & qui sub rege Stephano fuit Regni vestri status fidem plus quàm suf-ficientem facit.
units.tr: Armed with logic, you now gaze into the very secrets of nature, and most wisely so. For you know what befits noble and magnificent men, illustrious and princely men, and what is required for ruling happily. You know what the wisest men of old, Plato and Aristotle, pronounced about the happiness of commonwealths and kingdoms: that those commonwealths are happy whose helm is held either by philosophers or by those who philosophize. The present condition of your kingdom under King Stephen, which you have witnessed, makes this belief more than sufficiently credible.

units.la: Et certè, si nihil etiam ad feliciter im-perandum Philosophia conferret: omnibus tamen, in primis Magistratibus, & Viris Principibus, quos proprijs, non alienis, oculis videre decet, hac nostra tempestate necessaria esset: qua tot hæ-reses passim ubique grassantur: quarum sicut nulla fere sine Philosophiæ fuco & telis prodit: ita nulla nisi Philosophicis oculis & armis rite conspicitur & confi-citur, testis est priscum illud & nostrum sæculum.
units.tr: Indeed, even if philosophy contributed nothing to happy government, it would still be necessary in our present age for everyone, and above all for magistrates and princely men, who ought to see with their own eyes and not with other people's. For so many heresies rage everywhere in our time, and almost none of them appears except under the varnish and weapons of philosophy. Likewise, none can be rightly discerned and refuted except with philosophical eyes and arms. That earlier age and our own bear witness to this.

units.la: Ut igitur in arcana Naturæ, Magni-fice Domine, facilius penetrare queas, en flosculum quendam ex horto nostro Physico: exiguum illum quidem extrin-secus: secus: sed valde suauem & feracem: qui irrigante nobilissimo & doctissimo Stanislao Skorulio, & ipso Lithuaniae ornamento, tibi cum aditum ad Philo-sophiae penetralia parare, tum Lithua-niam totam queat locupletare. Si enim aliquid video, literatura breui solum versura, in Lithuaniam & Poloniam, quae tot nobis eximia ingenia profert, tam humaniter literatos excipit, concessura videtur.
units.tr: So that you may more easily penetrate the secrets of nature, Magnificent Lord, here is a little flower from our physical garden. It is small on the outside, but very sweet and fruitful. Watered by the most noble and learned Stanislaus Skorulius, himself an ornament of Lithuania, it can both prepare for you an entrance into the inner sanctuary of philosophy and enrich all of Lithuania. For if I can see anything, literature, which has only lately been turned over in Lithuania and Poland, a land that produces so many outstanding talents for us, seems likely to welcome learned men so kindly.

units.la: Eo itaque fruere, teque, Iohannes illustris, oblecta, dum integra totius Naturalis Scientiae, quam prae manibus habemus, Epitome subsequatur. Bene vale, & veram Philosophiam cum religione vera coniungere perge. Hædel-bergae io. Cal. Aprilis[?] MDXC.
units.tr: Therefore take your enjoyment of it, illustrious John, and take pleasure in it, while the complete Epitome of the whole natural science that we have in hand is to follow. Farewell, and go on joining true philosophy with true religion. Heidelberg, 23 March 1590.

units.la: FORTVNATI CRELII, PHI-LOSOPHI, DE SVBIECTO ME-TEOROLOGIAE, HACTE-nus incognito, Disputatio.
units.tr: The Disputation of Fortunatus Crellius, Philosopher, On the Subject of Meteorology Hitherto Unknown

units.la: SIC VT, imperfectè mixtum corpus Meteo-rologiae subiectum esse, multis ante nos cognitum fuit: ita quod nam tandem hoc imperfectè mixtum corpus sit, nemo post Aristotelem intellexisse videtur.
units.tr: Just as it has been known to many before us that the imperfectly mixed body is the subject of meteorology, so no one after Aristotle seems to have understood what this imperfectly mixed body actually is.

units.la: Alij enim hoc imperfectè mixtum corpus res illas esse dicunt, quæ tum in sublimi & aere, tum ad terram & intra terram generantur, puta, faces, cometas, niuem, pluuiam, flumina, & cetera id generis: alij geminum illum halitum, siccum & humidum: alij denique utraque simul, seu imperfectè mixtum, ut geminum halitum, & quæ ex eo generan-tur, comprehendit.
units.tr: For some say that this imperfectly mixed body is those things which are generated both in the upper air and on the earth and within the earth, for example torches, comets, snow, rain, rivers, and things of that kind. Others say it is that twofold exhalation, the dry and the moist. Others, finally, take in both together, that is, the imperfectly mixed body as comprising the twofold exhalation and the things generated from it.
But none of these can stand.

units.la: Illa enim, quæ ex gemino halitu tum in sublimi, tum ad terram & intra terram fiunt, subiecti locum obtinere non posse, non solum ex eo liquet, quòd quædam illo-rum, puta, pluuia, flumina, fontes, non mixta, sed sim-plicia, plicia, corpora, simplex aqua, sunt : sed etiam quòd in his Libris non affectiones horum, sed hæc, vt affectiones aliorum, cur hæc alijs, imperfecteque mixto corpori insint, inquiruntur.
units.tr: For that those things which come from the twofold exhalation, both in the upper air and on the earth and within the earth, cannot hold the place of a subject is clear, not only because some of them, for example rain, rivers and springs, are not mixed but simple bodies, simple water, but also because in these books it is not the affections of these things that are inquired into, but these things are inquired into as the affections of others: why these things, rather than others, belong to an imperfectly mixed body.

units.la: Nam quod Philosophus quatuor illorum, arcus, coronæ, parheliorum, virgarum, affectiones percenset, eorumque post causas exponit, id non facit, vt quatuor illa subiectum illius partis esse doceat (quo enim modo, quod revera non est sed esse dūtaxat videtur, naturalis Scientiæ subiectum fuerit?) sed vt ex his eorum natura plenius innotescat.
units.tr: For when the Philosopher enumerates the affections of those four things, the rainbow, the halos, the parhelia and the rods, and afterwards sets out their causes, he does not do this to teach that those four things are the subject of that part (for in what way could something that is not really there but only appears to be there be the subject of natural science?), but so that their nature may be better known from these.

units.la: Cum ergo non cometarum, pluuiæ, niuis, & ceterorum id generis, affectiones, neque cur his alia, sed cur hæc aliis accidant, Meteorologia perquirat : subiectum illius esse non possunt : cuius proprium est, vt illius tum principia, tum affectiones inuestigentur: quippe in quibus tota tractatio versatur.
units.tr: Since, then, meteorology inquires not into the affections of comets, rain, snow and things of that kind, nor why other things rather than these befall them, but why these things befall other things, these cannot be its subject. For it is proper to a subject that both its principles and its affections be investigated, since the whole treatment turns on these.

units.la: Hæc causa est, cur ista passim affectiones à Philosopho nuncupentur : quod non fieret, si subiecti locum obtinerent.
units.tr: This is the reason why the Philosopher everywhere calls those things affections; he would not do so if they held the place of a subject.

units.la: Et quò quæso modo subiectum huius Scientiæ fuerint quæcunque originem ex gemino illo halitu ducunt: cùm inter hæc quædam sint quæ nó corpora naturalia, sed accidentia duntaxat sunt, veluti terræ motus, tonitruum, fulgur?
units.tr: And I ask, in what way could whatever arises from that twofold exhalation be the subject of this science, since among these there are some which are not natural bodies but are merely accidents, such as earthquakes, thunder and lightning?

units.la: Sicut enim hæc (qua in parte quoque complures à vero absunt) è sicco illo halitu, ceu materia, non constant: sic originem suam ex eo ducunt: eo quod spiritus, qui aliud nihil, quàm fluens halitus est, vel intra terram fluens, vel è nube elisus & alias feriens, efficiens eorum causa est.
units.tr: For just as these things (in which respect also many are far from the truth) do not consist of that dry exhalation as their matter, so they do not derive their origin from it; rather, the wind, which is nothing other than a flowing exhalation, either flowing within the earth or driven out from a cloud and striking other things, is their efficient cause.

units.la: Certe, si nix, pluuia, & cetera id generis, huius Scientiæ subiectum sunt: etiam cum tria hæc, tum quatuor illa, quæ in aere apparent quidem, reuera autem non insunt, illius subiectum erunt: cum pari & eadem omnia ratione in ea considerentur.
units.tr: Certainly, if snow, rain and things of that kind are the subject of this science, then both these three and those four things which appear indeed in the air but in reality are not in it will also be its subject, since all of them are considered in it in the same and equal way.

units.la: Non magis geminus halitus subiecti locum obtinere potest.
units.tr: Nor can the twofold exhalation hold the place of a subject any more.

units.la: Primo enim, ut concedamus, utrunque halitum duorum elementorum conditiones participare, humidum humorem aquæ, calorem aeris, siccum siccitatem terræ, calorem ignis: hoc tamen nondum sufficit, ut imperfecte mixta dicantur.
units.tr: For, first, even if we grant that each exhalation shares the qualities of two elements, the moist the moisture of water and the heat of air, and the dry the dryness of earth and the heat of fire, this still does not suffice for them to be called imperfectly mixed.

units.la: Sicut enim ut perfecte mixtum quid dicatur, dicique possit, ex omnibus elementis, & his perfecte inter se permistis, ita ut permistione & mutua illa actione & passione diuersa natura constituatur, mixtum fit necesse est: sic ut imperfecte mixtum quid dici possit, è duobus minimum elementis constet, necesse est.
units.tr: For just as something is necessarily called perfectly mixed, and can be so called, when it is made of all the elements, these being perfectly intermingled with one another, so that by this intermingling and mutual action and passion a nature of a different kind is constituted, so something can be called imperfectly mixed only if it is necessarily made of at least two elements.

units.la: Quod cum de halitu dici nequeat: patet, eum imperfecte mixtis adnumerari non posse.
units.tr: Since this cannot be said of an exhalation, it is plain that it cannot be counted among the imperfectly mixed bodies.

units.la: Deinde falsum est, utrunque gemini elementi conditiones participare.
units.tr: Next, it is false that each of the twofold elements shares the qualities.

units.la: Vapor enim, de sententia Philosophi, naturâ suâ humi-dus est & frigidus, sicut aqua, ex qua secernitur, humida est & frigida:calescit autem partim vi Solis, à quo secerni-tur,& attollitur: partim à sicco illo halitu, quem sibi semper admixtum habet: qui, excrementum cùm sit , calidus est,etsi terra, ex qua gignitur,frigida est.
units.tr: For vapour, according to the opinion of the Philosopher, is by its nature moist and cold, just as the water from which it is separated is moist and cold. It is warmed partly by the power of the sun, by which it is separated and lifted up, and partly by that dry exhalation which it always has mixed with itself. This, since it is a residue, is warm, even though the earth from which it is generated is cold.

units.la: Atque hæc causa est, cur eundem illum humidum hali-tum Philosophus etiam humidum & calidum esse dicat.
units.tr: And this is the reason why the Philosopher says that the same moist exhalation is also moist and warm.

units.la: Nisi hoc dicamus:non video, qui contradiction ista tolli possit.
units.tr: Unless we say this, I do not see how this contradiction can be removed.

units.la: Illud vero, quòd neuter halitus merus & absque altero attollitur,non facit,vt vterque in se consideratus , mixtus esse dicatur.
units.tr: But the fact that neither exhalation is lifted up alone and apart from the other does not make it so that each, considered in itself, is said to be mixed.

units.la: Liquet ita,cùm neuter halitus imperfectè mixtum corpus sit,vereque dici possit:neutrum illud corpus esse, quod subiectum est Meteorologiæ.
units.tr: It is clear, then, since neither exhalation is an imperfectly mixed body, and since it can truly be said that neither of them is the body which is the subject of meteorology.

units.la: Quod ex eo quoque patet,quod Philosophus geminum istum halitum vbique principij loco statuit,de eo, vt principio,non,vt subiecto agit.
units.tr: This is also plain from the fact that the Philosopher everywhere posits that twofold exhalation as a principle, and treats of it as a principle, not as a subject.

units.la: Quid enim clarius illis Philosophi verbis de Ventis vero dicamus,sumtò illo, quod iam ante constituimus, principiò. sunt enim exhalationum dua, vt dicebamus, species ? quid item illis de fulgure autem & tonitruo , de typhone insuper, prestere, & fulminibus dicamus nam & horum omnium idem principium esse censendum est. cum enim haletus,vt dicebamus,geminus sit?
units.tr: For what could be clearer than the Philosopher's words: "Let us speak of the winds, taking as our principle what we established earlier. For there are, as we said, two kinds of exhalation. Likewise, what shall we say of lightning and thunder, and moreover of typhoon, prester and thunderbolts? For the principle of all of these is to be considered the same, since the exhalation, as we said, is twofold."

units.la: Eodem modo initio quoque Meteorologicæ Tracta-tionis geminum halitum principium & causam, & causam quidem ut materiam omnium eorum esse docet, quæ tum in ignis elemento, tum in ceteris procreantur.
units.tr: In the same way, at the beginning of the treatise on meteorology, he teaches that the twofold exhalation is the principle and cause of all those things which are produced both in the element of fire and in the others, and indeed as their matter.

units.la: Non potest ergo quod ut principium in aliqua Scientia parte consideratur subiectum illius esse.
units.tr: Therefore, what is considered as a principle in some part of a science cannot be the subject of that part.

units.la: Idem ex eo quoque clare patet, quod ut alibi docemur, nullum subiectum in sua Scientia demonstratur, sed utroque modo, & quid, & quod fit, præcognitum ponitur.
units.tr: This is also clearly plain from the fact that, as we are taught elsewhere, no subject is demonstrated in its own science, but both what it is and that it is are assumed as already known.

units.la: Quare cum Philosophus in Meteorologicis [illegible, ~3 letters]gemi-ni halitus demonstret, ut tum ex primo, tum secundo libro patet: planum est, eum Meteorologicorum subiectum non esse.
units.tr: Wherefore, since the Philosopher in the Meteorologica [illegible, ~3 letters] demonstrates the twofold exhalation, as is clear from both the first and the second book, it is plain that it is not the subject of the Meteorologica.

units.la: Et qui tandem eorum & affectionum illarum, quarum causæ in illis inquiruntur, subiectum fuerit: cum tonitrui, terræ motus, subiectum non halitus sit, sed nubes vel terra?
units.tr: And what, finally, would be the subject of those affections whose causes are inquired into in these books, since the subject of thunder and earthquakes is not an exhalation but a cloud or the earth?

units.la: Vanum igitur & præter rem, quod de gemini halitus principiis & affectionibus dicitur.
units.tr: What is said, then, about the principles and affections of the twofold exhalation is empty and beside the point.

units.la: Nec enim vel aqua, vel terra, è quibus geminus iste halitus excernitur, sed excretus halitus huius tractationis principium, & communis omnium quæ elementis accidunt, causa statuitur.
units.tr: For neither water nor earth, from which that twofold exhalation is separated, is posited as the principle of this treatise, but the exhalation once separated is posited as its principle, and as the common cause of all things that befall the elements.

units.la: Sic affectiones & accidentia, quorum causæ hic inquiruntur, non ipsi halitui, ut primo subiecto insunt, sed alij priori, halituque posteriori: quippe quod & halitu & elemento constat.
units.tr: So the affections and accidents whose causes are inquired into here do not inhere in the exhalation as in a first subject, but in another thing prior to it, and posterior to the exhalation, since that thing consists both of exhalation and of element.

units.la: Ex his autem simul quoque patet, cum neque geminus halitus, neque res illæ, quæ ex gemino halitu fiunt, puta, cometæ, faces, nix, pluuia, flumina &c. illud imperfectè mixtum corpus sint, quod horum Librorum subiectum est, etiam vtraque simul illud esse non posse.
units.tr: From these points it is also plain at the same time that, since neither the twofold exhalation nor those things which arise from the twofold exhalation, such as comets, torches, snow, rain, rivers and so on, are that imperfectly mixed body which is the subject of these books, neither can both together be that.

units.la: Neque tamen subiecto vacare hæc Scientia potest: cum ut in Posterioribus traditur, omnis Scientia in tribus verse-tur, in genere siue subiecto, in principiis, in affectionibus.
units.tr: Yet this science cannot be without a subject, since, as is taught in the Posterior Analytics, every science is concerned with three things: the genus or subject, the principles, and the affections.

units.la: Ut itaq; rē hanc, nemini post Aristot lem, ut videtur, cognitam, primi declaramus, dicimus, imperfectè mixtū hoc corpus & Meteorologiæ subiectū, neque geminum halitū, nec affectiones illas, sed medium quoddam inter halitum & affectiones, halitu quidem posterius, affectionibus vero prius, corpus esse, idque ex quatuor elementorum uno, & alterutro halitu constare, sed ita, ut halitus semper ex alio elemento fit, quàm illud fit, qui cum concrescit.
units.tr: So, in order to declare first this matter, which seems to have been known to no one since Aristotle, we say that this imperfectly mixed body, which is the subject of meteorology, is neither the twofold exhalation nor those affections, but a certain middle thing between the exhalation and the affections: posterior to the exhalation, indeed, but prior to the affections. It consists of one of the four elements and of one or the other exhalation; but in such a way that the exhalation is always made from an element other than that which is concreted along with it.

units.la: Sic enim fit, ut è duobus elementis constet, vereque imperfectè mixtum corpus dici queat.
units.tr: For in this way it comes about that the body is composed of two elements, and can truly be called an imperfectly mixed body.

units.la: Ita verò se rem habere, clarissimè ex iis perspicitur, quæ ex humido halitu seu vapore in aere generantur.
units.tr: That this is so is most clearly seen from those things which are generated in the air from moist exhalation, or vapour.

units.la: Attollitur enim vapor: qui una cum aere in nubem concrescit. huic ita ex aere & vapore concreto corpori, quod nubem dicimus, ubi naturam & perfectionem suam adsecutum est, accidit, ut modò quidem pluuiam exhibeat, modò grandinem aut niuem.
units.tr: For the vapour is raised up, and together with the air it condenses into a cloud. To this body, made of air and condensed vapour, which we call a cloud, once it has attained its nature and perfection, it happens that it now yields rain, now hail or snow.

units.la: Ea tria hæc: materiam (nam de efficiente in præsentia solliciti non fumus)halitum humidum, seu vaporem, & dein illam aeris partem, quæ in nubem cum vapore concrescit: subiectum, concretum illud ex aere & vapore corpus, siue nubem: affectionem, pluviam, nivem.
units.tr: There are these three things: the matter (for we are not concerned at present with the efficient cause), the moist exhalation, or vapour, and then that part of the air which condenses with the vapour into a cloud; the subject, that body composed of air and vapour, or the cloud; the affection, rain, snow.

units.la: Sicut, enim nubes ex affectionum illarum numero non est, nec vt affectio nobis ab Aristotele proponitur: ita vere imperfecte mixtu illud corpus est: quia duobus elementis constans, aere & aqua, seu vapore, qui aquæ est naturæ.
units.tr: Just as the cloud is not among those affections, nor is it proposed by Aristotle as an affection, so that body is truly an imperfectly mixed body, since it consists of two elements, air and water, or vapour, which is of the nature of water.

units.la: Nec quenquam turbet, quòd nivem, pluviam & cetera id generis, quæ substantiæ sunt, & corpora naturalia, affectiones & accidentia cum Aristotele facimus.
units.tr: Nor should it disturb anyone that we, with Aristotle, call snow, rain and the like, which are substances and natural bodies, affections and accidents.

units.la: Utrunque sunt: corpora naturalia, per & in se considerata: affectiones, ratione nubis concretique corporis: cui accidit, & quidem per se, ut modo quidem in pluviam, modo in grandinem aut nivem immutetur.
units.tr: They are both: natural bodies, considered in themselves and through themselves; affections, with respect to the cloud or condensed body to which they happen, and indeed through themselves, so that the cloud is changed now into rain, now into hail or snow.

units.la: Quæ horum ratio est, eadem ceterorum omnium est.
units.tr: Whatever the reason is for these, the same is the reason for all the others.

units.la: Sicut enim vapor cum aere concrescit, concretumque nobis corpus gignit, quod affectiones suas habet: ita sic-cus ille halitus, qui similiter continenter ascendit, cum igne concrescit, concretum ex igne & sicco illo halitu, eoque duobus elementis constans corpus, gignit: cui pro di-verso illius situ & multitudine accidit, ut modo hanc, modo aliam formam recipiat, lac, facem aut Cometam, repræ-sentet.
units.tr: For just as vapour condenses with air and produces a condensed body which has its affections, so that dry exhalation, which likewise rises continually, condenses with fire and produces a body composed of fire and that dry exhalation, a body consisting of two elements; and to this, according to its different position and quantity, it happens that it takes now this, now another form, and presents the appearance of a milky way, a torch, or a comet.

units.la: Atque hanc Philosophi mentem esse, ex eo clare perspicitur, quod passim in Meteorologicis, præter geminum halitum & affectiones illas, cōcretionis, συστάσεως ἢ πυκνώ- [?] ως[?], concrescentis & densescentis corporis, mentionem facit, quodque concretum hoc & densum corpus medium inter halitum & affectiones statuit, halitu scilicet posterius, affectionibus vero prius.
units.tr: That this is the mind of the Philosopher is clearly seen from the fact that throughout the Meteorology, besides the two exhalations and those affections, he makes mention of condensation, systasis or pyknosis (?), of the condensing and thickening body, and that he sets this condensed and thick body as a middle between the exhalation and the affections, being posterior to the exhalation but prior to the affections.

units.la: Quod cum primis ex illis verbis claret: fit igitur adspectu quidem reflexio, aere & vapore in nubem concrescente.
units.tr: This becomes clear especially from those words: "So there is a reflection in appearance, when air and vapour condense into a cloud."

units.la: En eadem tria nunc in Aristotele, quæ in aere ante monstrauimus: materiam, quæ vapor est cum aliqua aeris parte: subiectum, nubem siue concretum ex aere & vapore corpus: affectionem, adspectus reflexionem, seu emphasin, quæ in nube ob adspectus reflexionem apparet.
units.tr: Here are now the same three things in Aristotle that we showed earlier in the air: the matter, which is vapour with some part of the air; the subject, the cloud or the body made of air and vapour; the affection, the reflection of appearance, or emphasis, which appears in the cloud because of the reflection of appearance.

units.la: Eadem tria Philosophus in ignis etiam elemento statuit, cum ita loquitur, Cùm enim perspicuum fit, superum illum aerem ita concrescere, vt accendatur, accensioque ista modò quidem talis fit, vt flamma ardere videatur, modò vero &c.
units.tr: The Philosopher posits the same three things also in the element of fire, when he speaks thus: "For when it becomes clear that that upper air condenses so as to be set alight, and this kindling is sometimes such that it seems to burn with a flame, and sometimes..." etc.

units.la: En iterum tria: siccum halitum cum supero aere, hoc est, igne concrescentem: concretum ex igne & halitu illo corpus: huius affectionem, talem accensionem.
units.tr: Again three things: dry exhalation condensing with the upper air, that is, with fire; the body composed of fire and that exhalation; its affection, such kindling.

units.la: Atque hoc ex halitu sicco & igne cõcretu corpus, quod nubi proportione respondet, non purum ignis elementum, quicquid Græci dicant, illud est, quod fomite, ὑπέκ-καυμα, Philosophus appellare solet: quod tum ex septimo tum quarto, primi libri capite liquet.
units.tr: And this body composed of dry exhalation and condensed fire, which corresponds proportionally to the cloud, is not the pure element of fire, whatever the Greeks may say; it is what the Philosopher is accustomed to call the fuel, hypekkauma, as is clear from the seventh and from the fourth chapter of the first book.

units.la: Ait quidè, ignem οἷον[?] ὑπέκκαυμα esse: sed ὑπέκκαυμα absolutè non nisi concretionem appellat.
units.tr: He indeed says that fire is as it were a hypekkauma, but absolutely he calls hypekkauma only a condensation.

units.la: Pruinæ, roris, idem subiectum: quia concretio vnius dici.
units.tr: Hoarfrost and dew have the same subject, because they are said to be one condensation.
